questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A lyric essay that argues about its own lack of grounds
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a lyric essay gains by admitting its thin evidence
questions.stem: Halfway through the seminar, the tutor asks what a lyric essay gains by admitting that it has no evidence to stand on.

answer.exemplar: The admission converts a weakness into the subject of the essay. By telling the reader that the material cannot be researched, the writer makes the reader's own response to the absence the thing under examination, and the essay's structure, its circling and its images become a working method rather than a failure of research.

questions.explanation: The admission makes the absence of evidence the essay's subject, so its method becomes the argument. Calling it merely a weakness misses that the refusal is being examined rather than concealed.
questions.hint: Ask what the admission puts under examination.

questions.explanation: The final sweep reveals the purpose of the earlier labour, so the account shows change rather than a mere succession of tasks. Repetition alone is not the test.

answer.exemplar: A case the definition cannot hold is worth bringing because it shows where the definition was drawn too narrowly, which no amount of restating the definition can reveal. questions.stem: Revising a piece on her grandmother's kitchen, a student asks how a definition of that kitchen could be extended and where it stops.

questions.topic: A definition extended and where it stops
questions.learningObjective: Extend a definition and state its limit
questions.stem: A member describes a local custom, and the tutor asks how far the group's definition of it can be stretched before it breaks.

questions.learningObjective: State the condition under which a definition fails
questions.stem: At the seminar, a member says a definition stops working when it stops excluding what it was made for.

options.text: The claim is wrong, because a definition that excludes nothing is the most generous and useful one
options.misconception: judges a definition by how many cases it admits

options.text: The claim is wrong, because a term that excludes nothing is the safest one to argue with
options.misconception: mistakes caution for usefulness in a definition

options.text: The claim is right, because a term earns its use by telling the group which cases are not instances
The claim is right, because terms are made by agreement and agreement cannot be revised
options.misconception: makes agreement permanent and so rules out revision

questions.explanation: A term earns its use by telling cases apart, so a definition that excludes nothing has stopped being able to do the work it was made for. Generosity is not the measure of usefulness.
questions.hint: Ask what a term is for.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A description tested against a second visit
questions.learningObjective: Weigh a return visit against a photograph
questions.stem: Revising together, the group agrees that a second visit would test the description better than another photograph.

options.text: The agreement holds, because a photograph is a record of the past and the place itself is not
options.misconception: treats a photograph as the only record of what a place was

options.text: The agreement fails, because a photograph tests a description more strictly, since it fixes a single moment
options.misconception: believes a single fixed moment is a stricter test than a.

options.text: The agreement fails, because a visit repeats the writer's first experience and so proves nothing new
options.misconception: believes returning adds no new information at all

options.text: The agreement holds, because a photograph records one view while a visit tests the whole account against what.

questions.explanation: A photograph fixes one view at one moment, whereas a visit sets the whole account against what is now there, which is a stronger test. A photograph is a record of the past and the place is not.
questions.hint: Ask what each method can check.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A lyric essay that argues about its own lack of grounds
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an essay's lack of grounds may still be worth reading
questions.stem: A member asks what makes an essay's claim about its own lack of grounds worth reading at all.

answer.exemplar: It is worth reading because the refusal lets the essay examine something a research essay cannot reach: what a place does to the person who cannot pin it down. The absence of grounds is not a defect to be confessed and forgotten but the condition the essay is working under, and the writing shows how a mind behaves when its object refuses to hold still.

questions.explanation: The refusal opens a question that researched writing cannot reach, so the lack of grounds becomes the essay's working condition rather than a defect. Confessing and forgetting it.
questions.hint: Ask what the refusal allows the essay to examine.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: One opening sentence, two kinds of essay
questions.learningObjective: Explain what two essays with the same opening go on to do
questions.stem: In revision, the tutor presents two openings that share a first line and asks what each one goes on to do.

answer.exemplar: The shared first line puts a room in front of the reader, and the two essays then take it in different directions. One returns to the room and keeps recording it, so the piece stays a description of a place; the other moves from the room to a general claim about how such rooms are used, so the same sentence becomes the first move of an argument and the reader has to follow a different contract.

questions.explanation: The shared line offers a room, and each essay then uses it differently, which is what makes the two kinds. The contract with the reader differs in consequence as well as in content.
questions.hint: Ask what each essay does with the room.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What makes an account a process
questions.learningObjective: State what makes an account of a procedure a process
questions.stem: The group closes by asking what makes an account of a procedure a process rather than a sequence of tasks.

options.text: Cover the last paragraph and ask what the earlier steps were for, and a process shows where a list does not
Cover the last paragraph and ask what the earlier steps were for, which is a fair test of a process
options.misconception: restates the test without saying what it distinguishes

options.text: Count the steps, since a process is an account with more steps than a sequence would have
options.misconception: measures a process by the number of steps it has

options.text: Ask whether the account is accurate, since a process is an account that got the facts right
options.misconception: reduces the distinction to factual accuracy

questions.explanation: The synthesis offers a usable test, covering the ending and asking what the earlier steps were for, which separates a process from a task list.
questions.hint: Ask what the earlier steps were for.
